title: Shipped a commercial mobile game where AI did most of the heavy lifting: what that actually looked like
author: aagameshq
selftext:
Merge & Mortar is a merge + tower defense for Android, made solo in about 10 weeks with Godot 4. It's free on Google Play (rewarded ads optional, one Remove Ads purchase).



How AI was used, honestly:

\- Code: written with Claude Code. I worked in phases and play-tested each one before moving on. Every change had to pass a verification gate (import, parse, lint, 1,400+ automated tests, a headless smoke run), because in GDScript "it compiles" proves nothing.

\- 3D: Claude drove Blender through MCP for our own models; some towers, enemies and props came from Tripo AI and were cleaned up, re-rigged and recolored. Everything is rendered to 2D sprites.

\- 2D: the menu background, ground textures and app icon started as Google Gemini images and were edited by hand.

\- Audio: music and sound effects are generated procedurally in code, no AI audio.

\- Promo: the trailer is built in code (Remotion) from footage captured from the game itself.



What didn't work: green tests were not proof. A Remove Ads perk had passing unit tests but was never actually wired into the game for weeks, and our first ad-SDK build passed every automated check yet crashed on launch on a real phone. Difficulty tuned with a bot also misled us: it made hundreds of moves in the first seconds, so levels it called fair were lost in the first wave at a human pace, until we re-measured at about one move per 0.45 s and rebuilt the curve.



Google Play: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.aagames.mergekeep&referrer=utm\_source%3Dreddit%26utm\_campaign%3Daigamedev](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.aagames.mergekeep&referrer=utm_source%3Dreddit%26utm_campaign%3Daigamedev)

comments.author: Dignified_Cyclops
comments.body:
Did you not test on an actual device?

What testing process did you use to get through the testing requirements for play store approval?

replies.author: MrLollypop2434
replies.body: Not sure what he used but I can tell you my process. First of all, I signed up as a company because I have a company, so I didn’t have to go through 14 day internal testing period. I did couple of games, and regular lifestyle apps. For games, I would set an agent to test a game prior to me testing it. So for example, if I have a game with 1000+ levels, he would test every single level before handing it out to me. If the game has endless loop, same thing! So after he’s done with his testing, the next phase is to send app to myself and my girlfriend. She has more time than I do so she’s definitely a better tester than I am (thank God on her) and after we’re done with that, only then I go through uploading apk to Playstore’s internat testing. There we set up everything that needs to be done, test for 2-3 more days and if everything is good, publish. Trust me… make sure your games/apps work without any issues before you click publish so you can avoid bad reviews and wait for 2-3 days for updates. Sure, you’ll get bad reviews on a bad game regardless :)

replies.author: aagameshq
replies.body: Yes, every release candidate was played on a real phone (Redmi Note 14 Pro), plus emulators for the consent flow and tablet/foldable sizes, and about 1,600 automated tests run on every change. For Play approval, new personal developer accounts have to run a closed test with at least 12 testers for 14 days before production. I ran that from Oct 2 to Oct 16 with friends and people around me, so it's a small and friendly test group, not a wide range of devices.

comments.body: Oh yea, i can spot that as AI from a mile away. Not that you need to "hide" it being AI but still, i think we should strive to at least produce quality products regardless of how much work we actually put into them.

replies.author: aagameshq
replies.body: ¡Sí, justo ahí lo detectamos! 😄 Ese crash pasó en mi teléfono antes de publicar, nunca llegó a los jugadores. Esa es la lección del post: los tests automáticos pasaban todos, pero solo probarlo en un dispositivo real mostró el problema. Desde entonces pruebo cada build en el teléfono antes de subirla.
